# Chi-Square Distribution Critical Values

The chi-square distribution is used for several statistical procedures. For a chi-square test involving an $r\times c$ contingency table, the degrees of freedom are:

$$
df=(r-1)(c-1)
$$

The table reports **right-tail critical values**. For a selected significance level, $\alpha$, the area to the right of the critical value equals $\alpha$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-chi-square-critical
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| tbl-cap: "Right-tail critical values of the chi-square distribution."

library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

df_values <- c(1:30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100)
alpha_values <- c(0.05, 0.01, 0.001)

critical_values <- sapply(
  alpha_values,
  function(alpha) qchisq(1 - alpha, df = df_values)
)

chi_square_table <- data.frame(
  df = df_values,
  round(critical_values, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)

names(chi_square_table) <- c("df", "α = .05", "α = .01", "α = .001")

chi_output <- kable(
  chi_square_table,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  align = "cccc"
)

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  chi_output <- kable_styling(
    chi_output,
    latex_options = c("hold_position", "repeat_header"),
    font_size = 9
  )
} else {
  chi_output <- kable_styling(chi_output, full_width = FALSE)
}

chi_output
```

## Using the Table

1. Calculate the degrees of freedom.
2. Select the column for the predetermined significance level, $\alpha$.
3. Compare the obtained chi-square statistic with the listed critical value.
4. Reject the null hypothesis when the obtained statistic is greater than the critical value.

Chi-square statistics cannot be negative. If the exact degrees of freedom are not listed, use the next smaller listed value as a conservative classroom approximation.

## Worked Example

Suppose a contingency table has three rows and four columns. Its degrees of freedom are:

$$
df=(3-1)(4-1)=2\times3=6
$$

For $df=6$ and $\alpha=.05$, the table gives:

$$
\chi^2_{critical}=12.592
$$

An obtained chi-square statistic greater than 12.592 falls in the right-tail rejection region. An obtained statistic at or below 12.592 does not.

```{r}
#| label: fig-chi-square-critical-example
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Right-tail rejection region for df = 6 and alpha = .05."
#| fig-alt: "Chi-square distribution with six degrees of freedom and the right tail beyond 12.592 shaded."
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 6

library(ggplot2)

example_df <- 6
example_alpha <- 0.05
chi_critical <- qchisq(1 - example_alpha, df = example_df)
chi_data <- data.frame(chi_square = seq(0, 30, length.out = 1600))
chi_data$density <- dchisq(chi_data$chi_square, df = example_df)
chi_tail <- subset(chi_data, chi_square >= chi_critical)

ggplot(chi_data, aes(x = chi_square, y = density)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_area(
    data = chi_tail,
    fill = "grey65",
    color = "black",
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = chi_critical, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 17, y = 0.025, label = "α = .05") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 12.592, 15, 20, 25, 30)) +
  labs(x = expression(chi^2), y = "Density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

The degrees-of-freedom formula above applies to contingency tables. Other uses of the chi-square distribution may calculate degrees of freedom differently.
